segments.title: What Even Is DNA?
segments.hook: You have 6 feet of DNA stuffed inside every single cell in your body.
segments.script: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It's basically the instruction manual for building YOU. Every cell in your body carries a complete copy of your DNA. And if you stretched out all the DNA from just one cell, it would be about 6 feet long. Now multiply that by 37 trillion cells. Yeah.
segments.visual_cue: Zoom into a cell, reveal DNA strand, uncoil animation showing 6ft length

segments.title: The Double Helix
segments.hook: Two scientists walked into a pub and figured out the shape of life.
segments.script: In 1953 Watson and Crick discovered that DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder called a double helix. The sides of the ladder are made of sugar and phosphate. The rungs are pairs of chemicals called bases. There are only four: A, T, C, and G. A always pairs with T. C always pairs with G. That's it. Four letters write the entire code of life.
segments.visual_cue: Build double helix step by step, highlight base pairs snapping together like puzzle pieces

segments.title: How DNA Copies Itself
segments.hook: Your body makes 3.8 million new cells every second. Here's how they all get the right instructions.
segments.script: When a cell divides it needs to copy all its DNA. An enzyme called helicase unzips the double helix right down the middle. Then another enzyme called DNA polymerase reads each side and builds a matching half. You go from one double helix to two identical ones. It happens insanely fast and it's accurate 99.9999% of the time.
segments.visual_cue: Animation of helix unzipping, polymerase sliding along building new strand, speed counter showing replication rate

segments.title: Genes and Traits
segments.hook: Your eye color was decided before you were even born. Here's how.
segments.script: A gene is just a section of DNA that codes for something specific like eye color or blood type. Humans have about 20,000 genes. You get half from your mom and half from your dad. Some genes are dominant and some are recessive. That's why you might have your dad's nose but your mom's hair color. Your unique combo of genes is called your genotype. What you actually look like is your phenotype.
segments.visual_cue: Highlight gene segment on chromosome, split screen mom/dad traits combining, dominant vs recessive visual comparison

segments.title: Mutations — Glitches in the Code
segments.hook: One tiny spelling mistake in your DNA can change everything.
segments.script: Remember that 0.0001% error rate in copying? When a mistake happens it's called a mutation. Most mutations do nothing. Some cause problems like sickle cell disease where one single letter change in one gene reshapes your red blood cells. But some mutations are actually helpful. A mutation in the CCR5 gene makes some people naturally resistant to HIV. Evolution runs on mutations.
segments.visual_cue: Show base pair swap animation, normal vs sickle cell comparison, shield icon for CCR5 resistance

segments.title: DNA in the Real World
segments.hook: We can now edit DNA like a Word document. Should we?
segments.script: CRISPR is a tool that lets scientists cut and paste DNA with precision. We're using it to treat genetic diseases, make crops resistant to drought, and even bring back extinct species. Forensic teams use DNA to solve cold cases decades old. At-home kits let you trace your ancestry back thousands of years. DNA went from invisible mystery to the most powerful technology we have. And we're just getting started.
